Nurses remain structurally subordinated within clinical governance, resource allocation, and institutional decision-making. This discursive paper argues that this gap persists because three mutually reinforcing mechanisms remain intact: historically entrenched institutional path dependence, operational deficits in competency-based evaluation frameworks, and persistent gaps in how leadership translates structural and educational reforms into clinical authority. Applying a historical institutionalist lens, we trace how early critical junctures locked nursing into a doctor-led, nurse-subordinate configuration that subsequent reforms have failed to disrupt.
